How to apply
Entry requirements
Applicants are expected to have a First Class or Distinction Masters level degree, or equivalent, in a relevant scientific or technical discipline, such as computer science or mathematics.
Candidates who have only a Bachelors degree will not normally be considered. For candidates in possessions of a Master's level degree at Distinction, we also assess prior undergraduate degrees, for which the normal departmental acceptance level is 2.1 UK equivalent or above.
Please note that the departmental entry requirements are higher than the University's accepted qualifications. Therefore, meeting minimum entry requirements does not mean that you qualify for entry to the departmental degrees. Other departments at Imperial College may advertise different requirements, thus you may consider reviewing the broader University PhD degree offering if you do not meet the entry requirements in Computing.
Outstanding applicants without a Master's degree and applicants not meeting the normal acceptance level but with extensive post-degree industrial experience relevant to the research area may still apply. They will be expected to supply in their accompanying documentation clear evidence of compensating factors, such as professional experience on the proposed research topic, experience accumulated in research labs or during research placements, cumulative years of study, and authorship of high-quality publications. All applications we receive will be evaluated across these dimensions before making an admission decision. Please note that individual cases for exception due to lack of a Master's degree cannot be evaluated over the email; the department will instead assess the formal application once this is received and without a need for the applicant to contact us.
English language requirements
As part of the application process, you will be asked to show that you have met the University’s English-language requirement. The University postgraduate English entry requirement page describes how you can fulfill this requirement. Our Computing Research doctoral degree requires that students attain University's English requirements at Standard level.
Important dates
Please refer to the application deadlines highlighted in the PhD admissions page. Please also refer to the deadlines advertised on the scholarship page if you intend to apply to specific schemes.
Applying
General information on the application process is available on the University application guidance notes. As part of the application, you will be asked to provide a CV, a personal statement, and a research proposal. Please make sure to include in your application an indication of potential supervisors, we recommend that you list 3-4 supervisors to maximize your chances of being shortlisted for an interview.
Preparing your CV
Your CV should summarise your educational qualifications, and indicate any relevant research experience, internships or work experience. The CV should also indicate any publications with web links from where they can be accessed. You will be required to submit with your application full degree transcripts showing results for individual subjects for both your Bachelors and Masters (or equivalent) degrees. Your application should also be accompanied by at least two reference letters commenting on your suitability to undertake research.
Finding a potential supervisor
You can suggest in your application a number of potential supervisors, whose research may interest you. You should look at the research themes page for a brief overview of the research interests of our academic and research staff.
Please note that we will normally consider your application only after you have formally applied and your application has been received by the Department.
Preparing your personal statement
Please include with your application a 1-2 page personal statement. The statement should discuss your motivation for pursuing a PhD degree and how this fits in with your desired progression or career aspirations. It typically also discusses relevant work experience and skills, and why you chose our university, your target supervisor(s) and their groups, and a particular research area for your application.
Detailed information concerning the proposed research plan for your PhD should be included only in the research statement.
Preparing your research statement
Your application should be accompanied by a 3-4 page research statement. This should incorporate a brief description of the general research areas and topics that interest you, as this may be used to select suitable academics to whom your application will be circulated. Note that this document should not a personal statement on your motivation to pursue a PhD, its main purpose is instead to discuss the research problems that you wish to investigate. Motivation should be discussed in the personal statement.
Your research statement should also discuss:
motivation for the research (i.e. why the topic is important for the scientific community and/or the broader society),
research issues you intend to address during your PhD and
your initial ideas on the research methodology (e.g. what sort of simulation or experimental techniques) you intend to pursue to address the research issues.
The research statement should refer to existing scientific literature using bibliographic references and should be your own original work.
The research statement does not constitute a commitment to carry out the exact research work that you have described, as this may change after acceptance and discussions with your supervisor.
All statements are expected to be written by the applicant, without help from Generative AI (GenAI) tools.
Submitting an application
You can submit an application through the College online application system. Under Proposed studies, please select General for the Computing PhD Research Area options.
Interviews
After you submit an application you may be invited to a formal interview. Interviews may be held in-person, via video-conference (e.g., Teams, Zoom, etc), or on the phone.
The interview typically involves giving a presentation about one of your past projects, or discussing some papers that you have been asked to read by your potential supervisor. The interview is also an occasion for applicants to learn more about the potential supervisor research interests and her/his team. Some questions you may like to ask to your potential supervisor include (but are not limited to):
Would I be working mostly individually or as a member of a team?
What projects your team is working on at the moment?
How do you interact with your research students - e.g. whether meetings are ad-hoc, at regular times, one-to one, or group meetings?
Contact us
For further enquiries, please contact our PhD Programme Administrator, Dr. Amani El-Kholy.
